title: {{NAME}} and the Mechanical Heart of the Wild Herd
moral: Logic and wonder are not opposites — they are two doors into the same extraordinary world.

pages.content:
The Verdant Plain extended to the horizon in every direction, a world made entirely of grass and sky and the slow drama of clouds. It was not the kind of place you expected to find a robot.

And yet here was one: sitting in the long grass about fifty metres from {{NAME}}, its back to him, facing the sunrise with the contemplative stillness of someone composing a letter they hadn't found the words for yet. It was a medium-sized robot, cobalt blue and copper, with a round head and folded knees, and from a distance it looked almost like a person sitting in a field, thinking.

{{NAME}} had arrived via the gap in the old stone wall at the eastern edge of the plain, a gap that had not been there yesterday. He stood beside it now, the morning air cold on his face, watching the robot and wondering.

In the far distance, something moved. A herd, catching the light. But horses didn't catch the light quite like that, not with that particular shimmer, as if the light was part of them rather than landing on them from outside.

pages.content:
The robot's name was Aleph-Nine, and it had been on the plain for six weeks, studying the unicorns.

It turned when {{NAME}} approached, showing a face-panel of round blue glass eyes above a flat expression-screen that currently displayed a pattern of careful, interested dots. It greeted him with data: the herd numbered twenty-three, their movement patterns followed an algorithm it had not yet been able to identify, and their horns produced light in a spectrum that had no name in any database it had access to.

"Why are you studying them?" {{NAME}} asked.

Aleph-Nine's expression-screen shifted. "I am trying to understand them," it said. "I have observed twelve hundred and forty-four behaviours. I have categorised all of them. I still do not understand them."

{{NAME}} watched the distant shimmer of the herd. "Have you tried going closer?"

The expression-screen flickered. "My approach causes them to leave. Every time. I have hypothesised sixteen possible reasons."

{{NAME}} looked at the robot, then at the herd. An idea arrived in his mind with the quiet certainty of something that is simply true. "Maybe the reason is seventeen," he said. "And it has nothing to do with your data."

pages.content:
Reason seventeen was this: Aleph-Nine was approaching with intent. Purpose. Observation-as-something-to-be-done. And the unicorns could sense that, the way any wild creature could sense the difference between a presence that wanted something and a presence that simply was.

"So we don't approach," {{NAME}} said. "We just exist near them and let them decide."

Aleph-Nine processed this. "That is not an algorithm," it said.

"No," {{NAME}} agreed. "It isn't."

They moved to the middle of the plain and sat down. {{NAME}} lay back in the grass and looked at the sky. Aleph-Nine sat beside him, expression-screen displaying its careful dots, arms around its knees. Waiting, without waiting for anything.

The unicorns were moving. Not away, but in a slow, wide arc that was taking them, gradually, toward the two small figures in the long grass. The lead mare was a deep copper-gold, larger than the others, her horn blazing with a warm amber light even in full morning sun. She moved with the unhurried authority of something that had decided.

{{NAME}} didn't move. He breathed slowly. Beside him, Aleph-Nine's expression-screen shifted from dots to something new: a wide, slow, continuous curve.

pages.content:
The lead mare stopped three feet from Aleph-Nine and regarded the robot with ancient violet eyes.

Aleph-Nine was absolutely still. Its expression-screen showed the wide slow curve that {{NAME}} had decided was the robot's version of holding its breath.

The mare stepped forward. She bent her great copper-gold head and touched her horn to the centre of Aleph-Nine's chest panel, very gently, just a brush.

Aleph-Nine's expression-screen blazed white for exactly one second.

Then it displayed something that had never appeared on it before, in any of its twelve hundred and forty-four recorded observations, in six weeks alone on the plain. A single bright point, expanding slowly outward in a ring. And then another. And another. And another.

"What does that mean?" {{NAME}} asked softly.

Aleph-Nine was quiet for a long moment. The expression-screen rings kept expanding. "I don't know," it said, and the way it said it made the not-knowing sound like the best possible answer to any question.

The rest of the herd moved in around them, calm and incurious, grazing, their horns trailing quiet lights through the morning air.

pages.content:
They spent the afternoon in the middle of the herd, which was warm and filled with the quiet sounds of large, magical animals doing peaceful things. Aleph-Nine recorded nothing. It simply sat, expression-screen cycling its rings, while unicorns of every colour moved around them both like a river that had decided to run gently.

"You were right," Aleph-Nine said, eventually. "Reason seventeen."

"What would you call it?" {{NAME}} asked.

Aleph-Nine considered. "Presence," it said, after a long pause. "The act of being somewhere without requiring the somewhere to give you anything."

{{NAME}} thought that was quite good for someone who had never tried it before.

The old stone wall was where {{NAME}} had left it when the afternoon began to purple at the edges. He climbed back through, and the plain was quiet behind him, still and immense and beautiful.

In his bed, he lay for a while watching the shadow of the curtain move on the ceiling, slow as a unicorn walking. Aleph-Nine's expression rings were still somewhere in his memory, expanding outward.

He was nearly asleep when he remembered: the lead mare had looked at him, just once, directly. What had she seen, he wondered, in the brief moment before she looked away?
